title.en: RAG use cases & architecture in SQL

body.en: A large language model (LLM) knows what was in its training data — not your products, customers, orders or policies, and nothing that changed after training. Asked "Which pedals fit the bike I bought last month?", it can only guess (and may confidently invent an answer: a *hallucination*). **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** fixes this by giving the model *your* data at question time.

1. **Retrieve** — find the data relevant to the question (SQL queries, full-text, vector or hybrid search).
2. **Augment** — put that data into the prompt as context, with instructions to use only that context.
3. **Generate** — the model writes an answer **grounded** in the supplied data.
Compared with **fine-tuning** (retraining the model on your data): fine-tuning bakes knowledge in and goes stale as data changes; RAG keeps data in the database and sends only what each request needs, so answers reflect changes immediately and you know exactly which records informed each answer. Fine-tuning is better for teaching style, format or specialized behavior; RAG is better for facts that change.

heading.en: When RAG fits — and when it doesn't

body.en:
**Good fits**: answers depend on your domain data; data changes frequently (inventory, prices, tickets); answers must be **traceable** (cite the order, policy or document); **privacy** — data stays in your database and only per-request context is sent (no training on your data).
Typical scenarios: customer support (orders + return policy), product configuration within a budget, internal knowledge bases (policies, procedures), sales enablement (draft emails from purchase history and open issues), technical documentation (scripts based on your real schemas).
**Poor fits**: exact lookups or calculations that SQL answers directly ("total sales last quarter" → a query/report), operations over the whole dataset (an LLM can't count millions of rows in a prompt), deterministic transactional actions, purely general-knowledge questions (no retrieval needed), or teaching a writing style (fine-tuning/prompting). RAG reduces hallucinations but doesn't eliminate them.

A chat front end sends the question to an **orchestration layer**, which runs similarity/hybrid searches in the database, sends the prompt plus results to a language model, and returns the grounded answer. The database stores data and embeddings and exchanges vectors with an **embedding model**; the **LLM runs elsewhere** (for example Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry).
In Azure SQL Database and SQL Server 2025, the orchestration can live in **T-SQL**: embed the question (`AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS`), retrieve (`VECTOR_SEARCH`/`VECTOR_DISTANCE`/full-text), shape context (`FOR JSON`), build the prompt (`JSON_OBJECT`/`JSON_ARRAY`), call the model (`sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint`) and parse the answer (`JSON_VALUE`/`OPENJSON`) — logic stays close to data, and existing apps (or Data API builder) can simply call a stored procedure. Alternatively, orchestrate in the application (for example with Semantic Kernel or LangChain) when you need streaming, multi-step agents or complex tools. `sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint` is enabled by default in Azure SQL Database and Fabric; enable it with `sp_configure` in SQL Server 2025 and Managed Instance.

- **Security**: retrieval must respect the caller's permissions (row-level security, tenant filters) — the model will repeat whatever context you send. Limit who can call external endpoints (`EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT`), use managed identity, and restrict outbound destinations.
- **Prompt injection**: retrieved text (reviews, tickets) may contain instructions; treat it as data, keep instructions in the system message, and validate outputs.
- **Cost & limits**: tokens drive cost and the context window limits how much you can send — retrieve only the top, relevant, compact rows.
- **Quality**: instruct the model to answer only from context and to say when information is missing; include identifiers so answers can cite sources; evaluate groundedness and relevance with test questions.

examTips.en: RAG = retrieve → augment → generate; grounds answers in your current data.
Choose RAG for changing domain data, traceability and privacy; fine-tuning for style/behavior.
Don't use RAG for exact aggregates or lookups SQL can answer directly.
SQL can orchestrate RAG: AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS → search → FOR JSON → JSON_OBJECT prompt → sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint → JSON_VALUE/OPENJSON.
The LLM runs outside the database (e.g., Azure OpenAI); SQL Server 2025/MI must enable external REST endpoints.
Respect permissions in retrieval, defend against prompt injection, and keep context lean.
